title: Cohort Analysis and Trend Extrapolation
description: Master cohort-based reasoning, S-curve dynamics, and trend extrapolation to build more accurate growth estimates.

interactions.prompt: A SaaS company's Month-1 retention is 60% and Month-12 retention is 35%. If they acquired 10,000 users in January, roughly how many are still active in December?

options.text: About 6,000 users
About 3,500 users
About 2,100 users
About 1,000 users

interactions.teachingPreamble: Cohort analysis tracks a specific group of users over time rather than blending all users together. Month-12 retention of 35% means 35% of the original cohort is still active after 12 months — this is measured against the original cohort size, not the previous month's survivors.

interactions.prompt: A DTC brand shows these cohort retention rates — Month 1: 40%, Month 3: 28%, Month 6: 25%, Month 12: 24%, Month 18: 23%. What's the most important signal for forecasting long-term revenue?

options.text: Month-1 retention is too low at 40%
Retention flattens around 24%, indicating a stable long-term base
The brand is losing customers too quickly overall
Month-18 data is too far out to be useful

interactions.prompt: Spotify grew users at ~30% annually from 2015-2019 (75M to 230M). If you naively extrapolated 30% growth to 2024, you'd estimate ~860M users. Actual 2024 users were ~640M. What best explains the gap?

options.text: Spotify lost market share to Apple Music
S-curve dynamics: growth rates naturally decelerate as markets saturate
Spotify stopped investing in marketing after 2019
Currency fluctuations reduced international sign-ups

interactions.teachingPreamble: S-curve (logistic) growth models show that most products follow an adoption pattern: slow start, rapid acceleration, then deceleration as the addressable market saturates. Naively extrapolating peak growth rates forward is one of the most common forecasting errors in estimation problems.

interactions.prompt: When estimating future revenue from multiple cohorts, total active users at any point equals the sum of each cohort's original size multiplied by its ____ rate at that age.

options.text: Churn
Retention
Conversion
Growth

interactions.prompt: You're estimating a food delivery startup's 3-year revenue. You have strong data on cohort retention but weak data on new user acquisition trends. Do you anchor your forecast on retention-driven LTV or on top-line user growth projections?

options.text: Anchor on retention-driven LTV — it's your strongest data
Anchor on user growth — revenue is dominated by new cohort volume
Build separate scenarios for high and low acquisition
Use industry benchmarks for acquisition and ignore your weak data

interactions.prompt: A marketplace adds 50K sellers/quarter with 70% Q1 retention flattening to 45% long-term. After 8 quarters, approximately how many active sellers does the marketplace have from these cohorts alone?

options.text: About 400K — simply 50K × 8 quarters
About 280K — applying 70% retention uniformly
About 200K — recent cohorts at high retention, older ones at 45%
About 120K — most early cohorts have fully churned

interactions.teachingPreamble: Stacking cohorts is essential for realistic forecasting. Each quarter's cohort ages independently: the newest cohort retains ~70%, while the oldest approaches 45%. You sum across all living cohorts: roughly 50K×0.45 for old cohorts graduating toward 50K×0.70 for new ones. With 8 cohorts blending from 45-70%, the weighted total lands near 200K.

interactions.prompt: Rank these factors by their impact on a 5-year revenue forecast for a B2B SaaS company, from most to least impactful.

options.text: Net revenue retention rate (expansion minus churn)
New customer acquisition growth rate
Average initial contract value
Sales cycle length in months

interactions.prompt: The marketplace from earlier just launched in 3 new countries simultaneously, tripling its addressable market. How should you adjust your seller growth forecast for the next 8 quarters?

options.text: Triple the 50K/quarter acquisition rate immediately
Model new countries as separate S-curves with lower initial acquisition
Keep 50K/quarter — international markets won't contribute meaningfully
Apply a flat 2x multiplier to account for international growth

interactions.priorContext: Previously you estimated ~200K active sellers for a marketplace adding 50K sellers/quarter with retention flattening at 45%. Now the marketplace has expanded to 3 new countries, changing the acquisition and growth dynamics.
